Robert Koch. The German physician and microbiologist who identified the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis as the causative agent of tuberculosis, and who established the foundational principles for linking microorganisms to disease that remain central to microbiology today.

In 1882, Koch isolated Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the first bacterium definitively proven to cause a specific disease. This discovery validated the germ theory and launched a new era in medicine. To establish this proof rigorously, Koch developed what became known as Koch's postulates, the logical framework of experimental steps required to prove causation in infectious disease. An organism must be isolated from the patient, cultured in the laboratory, used to infect an animal, and then re-isolated from that animal. This methodology became the standard for all infectious disease research that followed.

Koch pioneered staining techniques that made tubercle bacilli visible under the microscope, particularly the Ziehl-Neelsen stain. As director of the Berlin Institute for Infectious Diseases, he trained a generation of bacteriologists who shaped modern microbiology. He investigated cholera and other epidemics, advancing both laboratory methods and epidemiological field investigation.

Koch believed disease eradication was possible through public health measures. His optimism drove tuberculosis sanatorium reform across Europe and influenced public health strategy for decades. In 1905, he shared the Nobel Prize with Paul Ehrlich. Both men were foundational to the theory that specific microorganisms cause specific diseases, and together they demonstrated that with the right tools, medicine could identify and attack these pathogens.
